messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Julian had been driving his sales route along the river valley when the skies turned black and the ground gave way. Rain fell in sheets, and within minutes, the water was at his door, then over the threshold. He remembered the cold, the roar of debris, the way the current pinned him to the dashboard until rescue finally pulled him out. The suddenness of the collapse and the sheer power of the rising water explained why specific environments now felt so hazardous. Now, months later, crossing the old gravel bridge or walking through the dense pines near his home sent a familiar jolt through his chest. Crossing the old gravel bridge or walking through the dense pines near his home did not just remind him of the flood; they pulled the fragmented record of that day forward. These spatial cues and the sight of untamed trees quickly deepened his conviction that he no longer knew who he was, making every ordinary location feel like a direct threat to his identity. That emotion, arriving without warning, quickly hijacked his nervous system. His heart would hammer against his ribs, his body would tense into watchfulness, and at night he would sit up to check whether he was safe, certain the flood was returning. The sudden terror on recall and the fragmented gaps made environmental cues feel unpredictable and potent, instantly reigniting the panic of the original event. The terror on recall and the widening gaps in what happened convinced him that he had fundamentally changed and that nothing in his life felt meaningful anymore. His fractured sense of self and the belief that he couldn't rely on others turned his nervous system into a permanent alarm, making him superalert and prone to flashbacks. This profound isolation and lost meaning amplified the gaps in his recall, leaving him with only a raw, shaking emotion that refused to stay buried. Believing he could not depend on anyone made every physical location and patch of woods feel uniquely dangerous, pulling his attention back to the environment. The exhaustion of remaining perpetually on guard and enduring repeated flashbacks reinforced his belief that he was permanently altered, stripping his daily life of purpose. Navigating the glass-walled conference centers and sterile office lobbies of his sales route now felt like walking through a minefield. He found himself suddenly superalert, scanning exits and feeling emotionally vulnerable to every unexpected client call. The sales territories he once navigated with ease now felt like threats to his identity, and his relationships had gone quiet. He stopped answering calls from friends, convinced they would only disappoint him or leave him exposed. He started missing client meetings, then taking sick days, until his manager pulled him aside. He knew he could not continue like this. Sitting in the quiet of the intake room, Julian admitted he was terrified of being alone with his thoughts, but he was finally ready to stop running from the spaces that had become so dangerous. He hoped, against his own skepticism, that someone might help him reclaim a sense of safety and show him what was left of himself.
